utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, will you call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-16-A, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Abell, I see you on your feet. I was going to open up by informing you of what I know about the progress of your motion. Do you have something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually, before we come on to that, I was going to mention on behalf of my absent colleague Mr. Clegg - I know that he is very anxious to be in court at the start of the proceedings, certainly at the start of the argument, which obviously touches upon his client - but Your Honours may be aware that he has encountered a problem this morning with Security to do with his pass. I don't know the details. I simply know it's the same pass he had proffered yesterday and the day before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right. We have been made aware of that, and what can be done is being done. He certainly can be in a position to hear the argument, and they're doing whatever they can do. But meanwhile we are going to proceed. Now, I take it Mr. Clegg's co-counsel is here; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: She is, Your Honour, yes. I merely said that because he asked me to say that. I know he's very anxious to be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sure of that, but we're not -- we do have to get the proceedings started. We are aware of the problem, and what is being done is being done here. Let me just inform you, Mr. Abell, about your motion. It has been brought to the attention of the President's Office. I don't have an answer for you yet, but one of our assistants is going to check at the break, at the 10.30 break. Now, if by some chance we are not able to get it by the time of your rebuttal, the Bench is willing for you, when you do get the answer, to make a written submission, if you care to, based on it, but not more than five pages. Hopefully something may happen during the proceedings before, but if not, you can attempt to alleviate that by the writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Pavkovic, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I merely wanted to inform you that my co-counsel Mitko Vrdoljak took part throughout the preparation of the defence. I would like to thank him. And I would like to inform you that unfortunately he died in a traffic accident last week. I would like to offer him my gratitude now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Pavkovic. We're sorry to hear that, and we acknowledge his contribution as well. Thank you for bringing that to our attention. Do you have something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. No, no, I have nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right, then, we will proceed. The Prosecution, by my count, has about two and a half hours left, if it needs to use all that. I think the way we will handle that is you can begin now and go for an hour and a half till -- that would be about twenty to eleven; then we'll take the break, the translator's break, till 11.00, and then after that you'll finish up your argument and then we'll go on to the rebuttals from there, okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will start off the morning with the part of the Prosecution's response in relation to the submissions made by Mr. Clegg pertaining to the additional Witness CA's statement and the impact of this additional evidence on the verdict. Your Honour, essentially the appellant has submitted that because you have on record two statements, Witness CA's statement and the rebuttal evidence that has been admitted by the Prosecution, he concluded that one of them must be telling the truth; and because the Appeals Chamber is not in a position to resolve these conflicting facts, he suggested that the case must be remitted back to the Trial Chamber for the resolution of these facts. The appellant, counsel for the appellant also made some comments to the effect that if Witness CA had testified about this telephone call before the Trial Chamber and Witness DD denied making that telephone call, then the Trial Chamber may well decide that Witness DD was lying and may acquit the appellant on Count 1. The appellant, Your Honour, is seriously not asking the Court to engage in speculation, because this is not the test that you apply at this stage of the proceedings. What the Appeals Chamber has to do is simply this: If the Appeals Chamber, by looking at the rebuttal evidence and the additional evidence, you cannot -- you are not in a position to decide one way or another which of these witnesses may be telling the truth or whether the additional evidence is reliable or credible, then you cast aside, you put aside the rebuttal evidence and you look at the additional statement by itself, taken it at its highest, you ask yourself: If believed, would this evidence have an effect on the verdict if this evidence was made available before the Trial Chamber? That is the test that one has to adopt at this stage of the proceedings. The Prosecution submits firstly that this additional evidence in the form of Witness CA's statement, whereby she speaks of a telephone call made by Witness DD and Witness DD asked her whether: "Do you know anything of my son and my husband, Nazif? Are they still alive?" Witness CA said, "I don't know anything about it." This statement, even if believed, does not render the conviction of the appellant for Count 1 unsafe. This is because the evidence of Witness DD pertains to a specific murder that was taken into account by the Trial Chamber as relevant evidence for persecution Count 1. Count 1, Your Honour, was an umbrella counted encompassing another murder and various other acts, the inhuman acts, and the murder count under Article 5. The test is whether it renders the verdict for Count 1, his conviction for Count 1 unsafe. The Appeals Chamber must decide whether this piece of evidence militates against the entire findings of the Trial Chamber leading to its final verdict in the conviction of the appellant for Count 1. The Prosecution submits that it does not, because there is still sufficient evidence for the Trial Chamber to make a conviction for Count 1, persecution. Not only does it not affect the verdict of guilt for Count 1, I respectfully submit that this does not, at the very least, affect the credibility of Witness DD even if you -- even if believed. Your Honour, the Prosecution has made extensive submissions in its response brief. May I just refer Your Honours to pages 51 to 54 as to why the additional evidence is not inconsistent with Witness DD's evidence, and I do not propose to go through them. I just refer Your Honour to those pages. Suffice to say, Your Honour, that even if the witness did make the telephone call to Witness CA two weeks after 16th of April, 1993, it cannot be reasonably inferred from that alone that Witness DD was entirely mistaken about her identification of the appellant's involvement or that she was completely lying about the appellant's involvement, his participation in the attack, and his conduct during the attack. I have summarised the material aspects, Your Honour, of Witness DD's evidence which the Trial Chamber relied on at pages 30 to 45 of my response brief. Your Honour, this additional evidence is not different. It's not evidence of a different character from that called at trial. It is simply further evidence which attempts to discredit Witness DD. The witness was subject to intense cross-examination, and there were various attempts made to discredit her by use of her previous statements. Witness CA's statement, Your Honour, purports to discredit her on one aspect of her evidence, whether she knew her family was killed. Then the appellant attempts to extrapolate from that that she could have not seen the appellant with a group of soldiers. The inference that he is asking the Court to draw from this statement is farfetched. It is not justified. And the question the end of the day is simply this: Would this piece of evidence if presented before the Trial Chamber and if the -- will it seriously affect her credibility to such an extent that the Trial Chamber will reject her evidence in its entirety? My submission is that it is highly improbable. There is no miscarriage of justice, Your Honour, if this evidence is disregarded. There was other and sufficient evidence available to convict the appellant. The appellant's motion for a retrial, based on this additional evidence alone, is entirely without merit and it must be dismissed. Your Honour, that concludes my submission for Witness CA. I will just very briefly, Your Honour, make comments, if I could, on the impact of Witness AT's transcripts on the verdict. I've been reminded that perhaps I should -- we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, the Prosecution is not seeking a remedy. We're not asking for a variation or revision of the sentence. We agree with my learned friend's suggestion that perhaps an obiter pronouncement as to the correct imposition of sentence for persecution and murder under the circumstances would suffice and is appropriate. We do not seek any other remedy, Your Honour. That concludes my submission. I am most grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Rashid.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: If Your Honour has any questions, I will be more than happy to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I don't have any questions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: I will now hand over the floor to my learned colleague Mr. Guariglia who will be responding to the appellants Mirjan and Zoran's appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Guariglia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I will try within hopefully 40 to 45 minutes to deal with the appeal of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic. At the outset, Your Honour, we have to make clear that it's very difficult to respond to an appeal of this nature, raising such a vast number of issues and mostly dealing with matters of weight of the evidence adduced at trial. I will only deal with what we consider to be the main, what we understand to be the main submissions raised by the appellants. All other points I will not touch upon. They have been fully addressed in our respondent's brief. Needless to say, I will be available for questions as to any other issue that has not been addressed during my presentation. Before doing it, it may be appropriate, although the Appeals Chamber is, clearly, fully aware of this, to bear in mind what appellant proceedings are not about. They are not about relitigating the merits of the evidence adduced at trial; they are not a forum to advance a particular interpretation as to what the evidence before the Trial Chamber establishes or does not establish; much less are appellant proceedings a forum to present misrepresentations of the trial record or allegations that do not find any support whatsoever in the trial record. In any event, one thing should be clear to the appellants: The time to advance arguments pertaining to the weight of the evidence before the Trial Chamber is over; the opportunity to persuade a trier of fact as to how the evidence before it should be interpreted is gone. The burden is on the appellants to demonstrate that the Trial Chamber erred either in law or in fact when making its decision. I will first deal with the common grounds raised by both appellants. The first common ground is the one pertaining to the indictment and the alleged error by the Trial Chamber in convicting the appellants of facts the appellants claim were not included in the amended indictment. The Appeals Chamber may remember the issue here are the events at Suhret Ahmic's house, the killing of Ahmet and Meho Hrustanovic, the arson of the Ahmic house, and the expulsion of the Ahmic family, which the Trial Chamber concluded were committed by the appellants. The appellants claim that this was not a component of the amended indictment and thus that they were prejudiced, that they didn't have sufficient notice to enable them to have an adequate defence and they were presumably surprised by the conviction. Now, the appellants have to demonstrate two things. On the one hand, they must demonstrate that the Trial Chamber erred as a matter of law in considering that these acts were included in the amended indictment, and at the same time they must demonstrate that they suffered prejudice because of the Trial Chamber's decision. The appellants rely mainly on a decision delivered by the Celebici Trial Chamber. I will start dealing with this particular decision. The reliance on the decision by the Celebici Trial Chamber is completely misplaced. The situation in that particular case was one in which the Prosecution, according to the Trial Chamber, had failed to adduce sufficient evidence to prove specific acts contained in the indictment and instead had adduced evidence that was immaterial for the purposes of those specific acts. In Celebici, the count involved the specific act of placing a fuse around the genital areas around a particular detainee - that was included in Counts 38 and 39 - and the Prosecution led evidence that related to different instances of victimisation of the same detainee. And there the Trial Chamber concluded, correctly so, that the charge was simply not proven because that specific act had not been covered by the evidence. The situation is clearly distinguishable from the present case, where the accused were charged with persecution in the manner of participation or aiding and abetting in the deliberate and systematic killing of Muslim civilians, the organised detention and expulsion of Muslim civilians, and the destruction of Bosnian homes and property, and the evidence adduced at trial led precisely -- was led at trial precisely to support those acts. So the evidence proffered went directly to the acts included in the indictment. Here we consider applicable to the case the distinction made by this Appeals Chamber in the Furundzija between the material facts underpinning the charges and evidence that goes to prove those material facts, and the appellants are clearly confusing both categories. Now, there can be no dispute that the events in the Ahmic house were relevant evidence of the persecution charge, showing the appellants' active participation in the persecutory attack, and that as such that evidence was properly led by the Prosecutor and correctly relied on by the Trial Chamber. Now, as to the matter of notice, no valid allegation of lack of notice may be raised by the appellants. In the Prosecution pre-trial brief -- sorry. To begin with, the indictment met all requirements under Rule 47 and Article 18, and it was expressly determined by the Trial Chamber that that was the case in their 15 May 1998 decision. In addition to the indictment that provided sufficient notice as to the acts that were attributed to the appellants, in the pre-trial brief, the Prosecution warned the appellants they had recently acquired evidence of individual acts of violence perpetrated by the accused and that such evidence was considered to be admissible as relevant to the Count 1 persecution charge. That was in the 13 July 1998 pre-trial brief, at paragraph 27. In addition, all relevant evidence pertaining to the events in the Ahmic house was fully and timely disclosed to the appellants. The trial record further shows that if there were any doubts remaining as to the scope of the Prosecution charge, its material facts and the evidence underpinning those facts, which should not have existed, really, those doubts disappeared on the fourteenth day of trial on 3 September 1998 when the Prosecution clearly explained the position in relation to the events at the Ahmic house, that those events were components of the persecution count; and this position was further clarified to the appellants by the Presiding Judge. And the record conclusively shows that counsel for the appellant Mirjan Kupreskic fully understood that the events at the Ahmic house would, in her own words, "be dealt with within the context of the persecution charge." This is the transcript at 1698. So the appellants simply cannot claim any surprise or prejudice. The question by the Presiding Judge, the first question that the appellants were invoking in their submission, the first question was a question for the purposes of having an absolute clarification as to what the nature of the persecution charge was. The final question at the end of the case is a question addressed to the Prosecution, asking whether the Prosecution considered that it would be appropriate for the Trial Chamber to rely on that particular evidence for the purposes of the persecution charge, which the Prosecution answered in the affirmative, saying, "Yes, it is perfectly appropriate for you to do so," and the Trial Chamber clearly shared this opinion. If, for whatever reason, the appellants considered that the manner in which the charge was pleaded and the manner in which the evidence was disclosed to them was insufficient for an adequate preparation of the defence, then the appellant had available remedies before the Trial Chamber. In particular, the appellants could have sought an adjournment of the proceedings, a remedy that has been recognised by the Tadic Trial Chamber indictment decision of 14 November 1995. The appellants completely failed to do so and, it must be assumed, they failed to do so because they thought it wasn't necessary. So there is no surprise, no prejudice that may be validly alleged by the appellants. This ground of appeal or this criticism of the judgement simply cannot be sustained. I will move now to other common issues raised by both appellants, and these are matters pertaining to Witness H. The appellants' basic submission must be interpreted to be that the Trial Chamber committed an error of fact by relying on the evidence of this witness for convicting the appellants, and there the appellants' allegations are basically attacking the credibility and reliability of the witness. Under the test recently developed by the Appeals Chamber in the Celebici case, it is for the appellants to demonstrate that the evidence could not reasonably have been accepted by any reasonable person, that the Trial Chamber's evaluation was wholly erroneous and that therefore the Appeals Chamber should substitute its own finding for that of the Trial Chamber. This is Celebici appeals judgement at 491. And absent such a showing, the jurisprudence of this Appeals Chamber is at this stage jurisprudence constante, that the Appeals Chamber will always give a margin of deference to a Trial Chamber's evaluation of the evidence and findings of fact. There are multiple allegations raised for the appellants made against this particular witness and, again, I'm forced to deal with the main allegations. The first one deals with prior inconsistent statements given by the witness. The appellant's criticism appears to be that the Trial Chamber relied on the evidence despite the fact that the appellant's testimony was inconsistent or had some inconsistencies with a prior statement that she had given to a investigative judge in Zenica. And further, that while giving evidence before the Trial Chamber, she denied ever having given such statement to an investigative judge. The response to this is very simple. The Trial Chamber was fully aware of these inconsistencies. This witness was vigorously cross-examined precisely on these inconsistencies. And taking these inconsistencies into consideration, the Trial Chamber concluded at paragraph 425 of the judgement that it had taken into consideration the criticism of her credibility arising from the discrepancies between her statement and her evidence and her denial of the signature of the statement but that, however, those criticisms were outweighed by the impression made by the witness upon the Trial Chamber while giving evidence. Now, the task of assessing the credibility and weight of the evidence before a Trial Chamber is the Trial Chamber's province. Inconsistencies or inaccuracies between prior statements and the oral testimony of a witness or between different witnesses are relevant factors no doubt for judging weight but need not of themselves constitute a basis to find the whole testimony incredible. The Trial Chamber in Celebici decided -- said at one point that when faced with a similar situation of inconsistencies, it had decided to attach probative value to testimony primarily on the basis of oral testimony given in the courtroom as opposed to prior statements where the demeanour of the relevant witnesses could be observed firsthand by the Trial Chamber and placed in the context of all other evidence before it. The Appeals Chamber, while reviewing the Celebici judgement, did not find any error in such a procedure and stated again that the Trial Chamber is the body in the best position to hear, assess, and weigh witness evidence. In the instant case, the Trial Chamber heard the witness, observed her reaction to cross-examination where all inconsistencies were raised and finally concluded that the evidence was credible and reliable. It further concluded that the witness was a forceful and confident one, paragraph 401. In addition to that, the inconsistencies contained in the -- raised by the appellants, the inconsistencies between the statement and the witness testimony, as far as the appellant's participation in the events are concerned is purely peripheral in nature. They do not alter the essence of participation of the appellant's in the Ahmici house. They deal whether the father had a rifle. Whether she had seen her father been killed by others or not, or whether she had heard a burst of gunfire and then she had seen the corpse of her father. They did not present any fundamental inconsistency as far as the events pertaining to the appellants were concerned. It was perfectly appropriate for the Trial Chamber to conclude that despite these inconsistencies, which were duly considered by the Trial Chamber, the witness was a credible one. The next layer of criticism to Witness H's testimony is that her evidence was illogical. It was illogical due to the visibility conditions that morning in Ahmici which would not have enabled any person to identify another person in -- under those circumstances, and thus the Trial Chamber erred in relying on this evidence. The appellants are mainly here relying on the evidence of other witnesses that, according to the appellants' allegations, certainly was extremely dark that morning and nothing could be seen and they rely, if I took note correct, on the evidence of Witnesses G, L, GG, K and C. Now, this issue was fully litigated at trial, and the Appeals Chamber may recall that there were attempts during the extensive Rule 115 litigation to relitigate again the issue on appeal. Witness H's evidence was that around 5.20 in the morning, one could see well. This is stated at paragraph 1754 of the transcript. The appellants should demonstrate that this particular assertion was totally illogical to the extent that it would be unreasonable for the Trial Chamber to rely on this evidence. Now, to do that, the appellants ought -- or to try to do that, the appellants present a falsely uniform picture of the visibility in the village at the relevant time as though all persons in that village at that point of time had exactly the same visibility conditions, would apprise the visibility conditions in the same way. They all could see exactly with the same degree of precision. Such an allegation or such a position does not find any support whatsoever on the trial record. For instance, Witness G said that it was visible because some houses were still burning. Witness E claimed that it was dawning at the time she woke up and looked up. This is transcript 1293 to 1294. Defence witness Milutin Vidovic said that about quarter past 5.00, you could see clearly but the darkness was receding and dawn was approaching. Transcript 7560. The appellant Zoran Kupreskic himself said that at -- that it was beginning to dawn at a quarter to 5.00, this is transcript 11282, and then added that when the shooting began, it had already dawned. It was daybreak. That is transcript 11289. So there is clearly no uniform lack of visibility. On the contrary. The evidence on the record shows that it was perfectly open to the Appeals Chamber to conclude that the visibility conditions were good enough for the witness to recognise both appellants. But in addition, the identification was firmly supported by the fact that the witness knew the appellants since the appellants were her neighbours, and this is, as far as I can understand, not disputed by the appellants. That she was only one metre away from both of them, and that in addition to their faces, she also recognised their voices. This is transcript 1639 to 1652. So the Trial Chamber's conclusion then that the witness had a good opportunity to identify the appellants and its decision to rely on the evidence is perfectly reasonable. The appellants have failed to show that on the basis of these alleged lack of visibility, the Trial Chamber's decision to rely on this evidence was an unreasonable one. I am aware of the fact, and I will deal with this very, very briefly, that the appellants also claim that, for instance she could have not recognised the voice of Zoran Kupreskic because she had never heard him shout. Well, that's not what the witness said, actually. When asked whether Zoran Kupreskic had addressed her in his normal voice, she said that the voice had been something in between a normal voice and a shout, and that Zoran Kupreskic did not need to yell when he opened the hatch since it was a small area. Then she further stated that the tone of the voice used by the appellant was sufficient for her to recognise the voice. And there is another inconsistency raised by the appellants dealing with an error committed by the witness who apparently thought that Zoran Kupreskic used to work in the Sutra shop. This is a minor confusion that is completely incapable of affecting the credibility of the witness testimony, and that was implicitly rejected by the Trial Chamber. The witness knew the appellants well enough for the purposes of identification. I will now move to the next criticism connected with the evidence of Witness H, and this relates to the Trial Chamber's decision not to call Witness SA. Your Honours may recall that there was also extensive litigation on this particular topic in the Rule 115 context. I can be very brief on this topic. The appellants' position is completely misplaced. At the outset, no accused, no party, I would say, has a right to have the opposing party calling evidence in the system of the International Tribunal. No party has an entitlement to have evidence called by the Court under Rule 98, because Rule 98 is an authority given to the Court in order to enable a Trial Chamber to call that evidence that a Trial Chamber perceives to be relevant for the ascertainment of the truth, but it's not a device to allow parties to supplement their cases. As it is totally clear on the basis of the record, the appellants were notified of the fact that the Trial Chamber was not going to have that witness heard as a Court witness, as had been expected and further, the Presiding Judge notified the appellants of their right to have that witness called during their case in chief, if they so desired, which the appellants voluntarily decided not to do in the expectation that the Trial Chamber would rely on the statements that had been admitted into evidence. Now, here we rely on this Appeals Chamber 8 May 2001 decision on additional evidence: "A Defence has no right to assume what a Chamber will or will not accept in making its findings. It must put forward its best case in the first instance." The appellants were not misled into believing anything. The appellants made a conscious decision not to that that witness called in their case in chief, and then they simply made a wrong assumption. That is not a ground of appeal. That cannot be a ground of appeal before you. It was perfectly open for the Trial Chamber to determine what weight, if any, it would attach to that material. The appellants should show the Trial Chamber abused its discretion by not attaching any weight to the written statements, and we will simply submit, for the sake of economy, that that decision was a perfectly appropriate one and that no valid criticism may be raised. Your Honour, there are more things that could be said on this point. I will only make a brief reference to finish with Witness H, a couple of minor points dealing with Witness H. One, the issue of whether the Trial Chamber correctly followed the principles laid down in an English case, Regina versus Turnbull. At the outset, no Chamber of the International Tribunal is bound to consider any case from any particular domestic jurisdiction, and that is a solid point. This having been said, it is clear at paragraph 339 of the judgement the Trial Chamber did consider the case in question, and it did understand and share the principles laid down in the said decision and was clearly alert of the dangers inherent in identification evidence. The Trial Chamber's conclusion by accepting Witness H was that those dangers were simply not present in the instant case, and that is the prerogative of the Trial Chamber which is the body in the best position to determine whether those dangers were applicable to the case, to the witness in question. The Trial Chamber, if it looks at other decisions taken in relation to witnesses in the judgement, like a decision not to rely on the evidence of Witness G or in the evidence of Witness C, will conclude that the Trial Chamber did exactly what it had to do. In the cases where they thought the identification was unreliable, it did not rely on the evidence. Where the Trial Chamber considered that those dangers were not present, it did rely on the evidence and no flaw can be identified in this particular exercise. One brief word about an allegation that was made on Monday as to lack of compliance by the Prosecution with Rule 68. An allegation of breach of Rule 68 is a serious matter. It cannot be raised light-handedly. The only material that the Prosecution had in its possession pertaining to Witness H was that statement which was disclosed to the appellants together with other material related to other witnesses. This allegation is raised with no substantiation whatsoever for the first time last Monday on appeal. The appellant had in his possession all the material during trial that enabled him now to make this speculative accusation of lack of compliance with Rule 68, exactly the same material. He -- the appellant could have, if that was his position, compared the material that had been disclose pertaining to other witnesses and the material that had been disclosed in relation to Witness H and raised at least a concern as to lack of compliance with Rule 68 during trial. The appellant did not do it. There was never an allegation at trial of a lack of compliance with Rule 68 in relation to Witness H, and the reason why there was none is because there was no breach of Rule 68. All the material that the Prosecution had in its possession was duly disclosed, and I have confirmed this between Monday and today. I will finish this only by saying that allegations of this type, with no substance whatsoever, simply should not be raised before the Appeals Chamber of the International Tribunal. There is one brief point raised by the appellants, and I will only need to discuss that in one second, dealing with the presence of BiH military units in Ahmici. That hasn't been -- that has been fully discussed in our respondent's brief so I need not spend too much time on this. But I will only say that the appellants appear to be arguing that the Trial Chamber erred in not concluding that there was some military presence in Ahmici on 16 April 1993. Now, interestingly enough, the appellants do not attach any consequence to this error. They do not explain what possible consequence this error could have. In the light of the crimes the appellants were convicted of, the Trial Chamber's finding was that what happened on 16 April 1993 was a persecutory attack directed against a civilian population, and heard abundant and overwhelming evidence as to the fact that the targets were the Bosnian Muslim civilians and that the property burned was Bosnian Muslim civilian property and that all casualties were Bosnian Muslim civilian casualties. I need not entertain this matter any longer, just to say that the Trial Chamber's findings on this particular issue are conclusive. The appellants, other than pure speculation, are not offering anything, and, as I said at the beginning, they don't even explain what the consequences of this error would be. I will move now to the last ground of appeal that is common to both appellants, and that one deals with the participating forces during the 16 April 1993 attack. Now, the appellants are claiming that, on the basis of the evidence before the Trial Chamber, the Trial Chamber should have concluded that only the military police and, within the military police, the so-called Jokers were responsible for the attack, and that no regular HVO forces, and notably the Vitez Brigade, would have been involved. Now, there is absolutely nothing on the trial record that supports such a conclusion. No error can be raised against the Trial Chamber's decision -- the Trial Chamber's conclusion, rather, that there was a broad range of HVO forces involved in the attack, including but not limited to elements of the military police, and in particular the Jokers. The appellants are relying on a number of orders and documents. I shan't bother Your Honours with details. They are orders from Colonel Blaskic, Exhibits D37 and D38. The appellants tried to construe an argument on the basis of this order, saying that the orders were clearly only directed to the military police. This doesn't hold water. The orders are addressed to a number of brigade commanders, including the commander of the Viteska Brigade, Mario Cerkez. Both orders include a number of duties which should be performed by the different brigades, including the Vitez Brigade. And further, Witness CI clearly confirmed that -- at least Exhibit D38 was an order to occupy the defence region and to block the village, addressed to the commander of the Vitez Brigade, Mario Cerkez. In addition, the Trial Chamber had before it a certificate of wounding, stating that the HVO Vitez Brigade member Nikola Omazic had been wounded during the 16 April 1993 Ahmici operation, and the Trial Chamber also had before it evidence showing clearly the involvement of the HVO Home Guard Commander, Nenad Santic, during the attack and before the attack. All this evidence was before the Trial Chamber. The references to the transcript are included in our respondent's brief so I need not waste time now reading them out to Your Honours. But in any event, what is clear is that the Trial Chamber had sufficient material before it to enable it to conclude that HVO regular forces had been involved in the attack. As to this reliance in the Kordic Trial Chamber's findings that the Vitez Brigade was not involved, the first thing is that particular judgement is currently under appeal and one of the reasons is that particular finding; and second, the relevant issue here is the Trial Chamber's conclusions on the basis of the evidence before it. And against that reliance on the Kordic judgement, I could, for instance, rely on the Blaskic judgement where, at paragraph 400, it concludes clearly and conclusively that the Viteska Brigade was involved in the Ahmici attack. I will now turn to certain specific allegations raised by counsel for Zoran Kupreskic dealing with the findings of the Trial Chamber as to the appellant's military status. The first thing is the weight of the eight documents that have been admitted by Your Honours. Our position is well known to Your Honours. It was expressed in the -- during the Rule 115 litigation, in particular during the 30 March 2001 hearing, and we stand by that position. Those documents relate to a different and higher level of military hierarchy. The only argument that the appellant is advancing to support his position that the documents render the verdict unsafe is that the name of the appellant doesn't show in any of these documents. Our position is that the name of the appellant need not appear in any of these documents since the appellant was involved at a lower level of military hierarchy. The interesting thing is that the appellant appears now to be denying that such a level ever existed, which appears to contradict the appellant's own position both at trial and on appeal. In his closing brief, the appellant, after asserting that there could be different types of commanders and several commanding levels - this is Registry page 5781 to 5782 - the appellant considered that he had had a role as a local coordinator of the village guards, but he claimed that that role was transferred to Dragan Vidovic sometime before the 16 April 1993 attack, an argument that was raised again in the appellant's appeal brief. The Prosecution's position is that the Trial Chamber had evidence, significant evidence before it allowing it to conclude that there existed a local level of command within the HVO structure. This evidence includes the activities of Nenad Santic, the HVO Home Guard commander; the appellant's signing as a representative of the HVO Santici of an agreement on 20 October 1992 with the Muslims of Ahmici, which was tendered as an exhibit at trial; the involvement of Slavko Papic, who was the Vitez Brigade 1st Company Commander with elements of the village guard. All this showed, among other pieces of evidence, all this showed that there was a local HVO structure and there was sufficient evidence, which I will now move to, indicating that the appellant had a commanding role in that HVO structure. First thing, you have the evidence of -- as to this particular point, the evidence of Witness JJ, the evidence of Witness B, that told the Trial Chamber how Nenad Santic had clearly stated to him that the appellant was the village commander or was the commander in that particular area; the evidence of Abdulah Ahmic, the evidence of Witness I, all evidence showing that the appellant had a commanding role within the local HVO structure. Now, there is one point raised by the appellant as to the fact that all this evidence dealt with the 20 October 1992 conflict and the aftermath of that conflict, but at the relevant time of the attack, the 16 April 1993 attack, there was no evidence showing that he still had a leading or commanding position. That allegation is plainly wrong. The evidence of Witness JJ clearly showed that approximately a month before the attack, the appellant was an HVO commander with an area of responsibility, being the chief person to organise the army in that area, and issued weapons, and further, that the area included the village of Ahmici. So our position there is that it was perfectly open, on the basis of the evidence before it, to the Trial Chamber to conclude that a local HVO structure existed, that the appellant had a leading or commanding role in that HVO structure, and to conclude further, that that leading or commanding role should attract enhanced punishment. The appellants have failed to show any error in this respect. The eight documents adduced as additional evidence cannot simply produce any effect whatsoever on these conclusions. Now that I mentioned JJ, and I think I will have to speed up and finish my submissions within the next five to ten minutes -- five minutes, hopefully, the video adduced in evidence also needs to be addressed. The video, the appellants claim, reflects the same oath-taking ceremony watched by Witness JJ. The appellant offers, however, no precision as to the date and time of the ceremony registered on tape. The video was simply proffered together with the appeal brief. Now, only for the purposes of the argument, let us assume that the video is precisely what it purports to be. What does that show? What impact could that have on the verdict? If that video shows what it purports to show, that would only imply that Witness JJ was wrong on this particular issue. It would not affect the rest of Witness JJ's evidence, much less would it affect all the other evidence that was before the Trial Chamber pertaining to the appellant's command position. As to how it would affect the evidence of Witness JJ, neither the appellant while giving evidence at trial nor counsel for the appellant today are submitting that she was an incredible witness, that she meant ill, that she wanted to prejudice the appellant, that she was a compulsive liar, or any other serious flaw to her credibility. The appellants' position while giving evidence was that the witness had mixed up some things. You heard from counsel for the appellant on Monday that she was confused about some things. Well, about how many things can this witness be confused? Let us assume that she was confused about the oath-taking ceremony. Does that necessarily mean that she was also confused about the admissions that the appellant made to her pertaining to his commanding status? Does that also mean that she must have been confused necessarily as to the ID that the appellant gave to her which said "Zoran Kupreskic, Commander"? She was clearly a credible witness, and it has not been alleged otherwise. The appellants have only been able to indicate minor inconsistencies in her testimony, such as the fact that she could not remember which HVO commander had signed a particular certificate, or that she could not remember whether Zoran's ID contained a photograph or not. She recognised at all times the fact that the appellant had asked -- had helped her out in difficult times, and she was grateful for that. She testified about her problems coming to testify, including pressures and threats once it was found out that she was going to come to testify before the International Tribunal. There is nothing on the record that shows that she was an inherently unreliable witness or that she had any other flaw as to her credibility. So our primary submission is that even accepting this video as a video of the oath-taking ceremony, that only removes a tiny portion of the evidence before the Trial Chamber underpinning its finding as to the appellant's command position. It doesn't affect the rest of the evidence, including the rest of Witness JJ's testimony, and therefore that evidence would not affect the verdict. Having said this, it is our position that Your Honours may validly ask yourselves whether this video, presented the way it was, would be relied upon by any Trial Chamber. Your Honours stated on your 26 February 2001 decision on additional evidence while admitting this video: "If the appellants are correct in this assertion, that this video depicts the same oath-taking ceremony in Vitez referred to by Witness JJ and, indeed, Zoran Kupreskic is a spectator rather than a participant, then this evidence could have had an effect upon the Trial Chamber's findings at trial." Paragraph 106 of Your Honours' decision. Now, let's see how this video was proffered. There is not even a letter, let alone an affidavit or any other form of evidence of the person purportedly taking this video indicating when this video was shot, what event was being recorded on video. It hasn't been authenticated by anybody. There is not even a date in the video that would at least give us a point of departure to make some assessment as to the reliability of the evidence. There is simply no material whatsoever provided by the appellants establishing that this is the same oath-taking ceremony referred to by Witness JJ. Now, I can't forecast what counsel for the appellants is going to say but we can ask for that material that if we wanted to have more evidence on the video we could have done it. That completely misses the point. It is for the appellants to demonstrate that the evidence would render the verdict unsafe. It is for the appellants to present before the Appeals Chamber the best material evidence of the highest quality that would allow the Appeals Chamber to make a determination as to that evidence would or would not render the verdict unsafe. In our submission, Your Honours may validly conclude after looking at the manner in which this video was proffered that this piece of evidence falls into that low category of evidence that was eloquently defined by my learned friend Mr. Clegg as evidence such that no reasonable Tribunal could have been influenced by it. Your Honours, I will very briefly move to one point because there's not much more -- I don't have any time left -- raised by Mirjan Kupreskic, and this pertains to the issue of mobilisation of the appellant, his involvement within the HVO. There is absolutely nothing in the appellant's submissions indicating any error by the Trial Chamber in reaching its conclusions as to Mirjan Kupreskic's involvement with the HVO, his position as a reservist, and his mobilisation for the purposes of the 16 April, 1993 attack. The allegations contained in the appeal brief had been advanced before Your Honour sorrily are simply recast submissions that were placed before the Trial Chamber. Basically the same defeated position, the same defeated arguments are being raised de novo before Your Honours. There are two minor things that I will say -- one, rather. The interpretation of the exhibits that showed the appellant was a reservist and that the appellant was mobilised, or the appellant was in a list of the HDZ, that was Exhibit 371, exactly the same allegations raised at trial. Exactly the same line of argumentation. They are putting before Your Honours that these exhibits meant something else, and that as told that was a conclusive finding they could reach on the basis of the evidence. That was a theory attempted by the Defence to explain the documents. Some Defence witnesses gave evidence trying to discredit the accuracy of these exhibits. They were vigorously cross-examined, and their evidence was rejected by the Trial Chamber. There's nothing in the appellant's submissions indicating an error of fact in the Trial Chamber's decision. I will give only one clear example: The appellant is telling you that the fact that the appellant appears in a list of HVO members is in contradiction with the fact that according to a different exhibit, he was mobilised on the day of the attack. Well, actually, according to the Defence witness, Dragan Majstorovic, the initial exhibit, the one of the HVO list contained a list of reservists that were highlighted with a "P" which involves were members of the village guards which were considered to be reservists. The name of the appellant Mirjan Kupreskic indicating with a P indication his condition of HVO reservist and probably his other condition of village guard. The subsequent exhibit simply indicates that the appellant was mobilised on 16 April 1993. There is no contradiction whatsoever between both exhibits, and the same witness I was referring to clearly established that a reservist had the status and been mobilised and became an active soldier. There is, other than speculation, as to where the appellant would have gone had he been mobilised other than raising again interpretations of the evidence that were unsuccessfully attempted before the Trial Chamber. There is nothing in the appellant's argument that would justify appellate review of the judgement. Your Honour, there is one last minor issue that I will need to address in private session, only one or two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I have two questions for you. I want to understand -- in your argument about the indictment and persecution, the beginning of your argument, I want to make sure I understand: Is it your argument that if the indictment alleges persecution in the form of killing civilians, burning houses, those kinds of allegations, is it your submission that the indictment need not contain anything more specific in the form of the incidents naming the people that were killed or the houses that were burned, et cetera? It's enough to just -- so long as you provide somewhere along the line in the trial information saying, "We're going to rely on the fact that it was X's house or that you appeared at Y's," but that doesn't -- none of that has to be in the indictment? That seems to run a little bit counter of some of the Tribunal's decisions that require annexes setting out specific incidents to pinpoint what the general allegations are.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Let me put it this way: In the Furundzija decision, vis-a-vis the decision was made between evidence pertaining to the material facts contained in the indictment and the material facts contained in the indictment, our position would be that -- especially with charges such as genocide or persecution which amount, you know, a vast number of instances of different instances of victimisation, it would not be practicable, it would -- in most of the cases it would not be possible to put all evidence pertaining to those counts in the indictment itself. Now, in the case of murder, clearly, you need to put a list of the individuals that you have killed. That's a natural consequence of the crime that you are pleading as a Prosecutor. But as far as crimes of persecution are concerned, then basically the Prosecution -- the indictment for previous requirements of providing notice by describing which acts the Prosecution considered to amount to persecution, and then it was a matter of disclosure of the evidence at trial or before trial much. Now, it may well be that the practice of the Tribunal has moved into one of more detailed indictments, but the question before Your Honours is was the indictment so pleaded fatal for the Defence, or was the Defence in notice of what the nature of the persecution charge was. And our position is, and I feel the record clearly reflects that, that the appellants fully understood the nature of the persecution charge and it was clear that the persecution charge involved the events in the Ahmic house.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: -- and the killing of Muslims. The evidence of Witness H or Witness KL was timely disclosed for the appellants. The appellants were either charged with a murder count or with a persecution count. Now, when evidence of Witness H was disclosed, that was clearly not evidence for a murder count because it involved an altogether different incident. It could only go to the persecution count. So the mechanics of the process of indictment, notice in the pre-trial brief, and disclosure of the evidence provided before trial sufficient notice for the accused. And if there was any doubt, yes, those doubts should have disappeared at the 14th day at trial and if there was -- if the appellants thought that that the manner which the charge had been pleaded did cause them prejudice, they should have asked for an adjournment. utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have the benefit of being the penultimate speaker with regard to this appeal, and I come at a time when my colleagues have expressed various opinions on the law and in relation to various witnesses. And this, to a large extent, may impact on the breadth and scope of my submissions in that I will be trying to limit it to pertinent issues relevant to the case of Vlatko Kupreskic and as far as it impacts on the finding of the Trial Chamber in the final analysis. I think it is important, however, that before I begin with an analysis of what are the issues, that it is important to appreciate the rule and responsibility of an Appeal Chamber a committance to the dictates of the ICTY statute. To that extent, it is important to keep in mind that the appeal proceeding in the Tribunal is of a corrective nature, and so far as the Statute is concerned, an appeal does not involve a trial de novo. The starting process of any appeal determination must be, and I repeat must be that the decisions of a Trial Chamber of this Tribunal unless reversed or revised on appeal are correct and, therefore, the party that is exercising or invoking the endemic rights of an appeal or in the capacity as an appellant must be able to establish the existence of an error within the designated Article 25(1) of the Statute. It is conceivable that sometimes there may be, indeed, an overlap in terms of whether the particular appellant is putting forward submissions in law or putting forward submissions that amount to error of law or error of fact. It is my rather uncomfortable responsibility to weigh through a plethora of facts since, in the case of Vlatko Kupreskic, it is in fact an appeal that is based on an error of fact. In other words, an error of the Trial Chamber relating to the factual conclusions it drew from the evidence presented to it. In other words, the trier of fact in the proceedings before the Tribunal consisting of those three judges who issued written reason decisions, the question on appeal is whether the evidence cited by the Trial Chamber reasonably supports the Trial Chamber's conclusions and, if so, the Trial Chamber's decision is entitled to deference even if others might have reached a different conclusion on the same evidence. It is only where the evidence cited by the Trial Chamber cannot reasonably support the conclusion it reached that the Appeals Chamber must appropriately intervene. I think to essentially skirt and circumscribe the role of the Appeals Chamber, I think, it is important to simply quote from the Tadic judgement that to my mind encapsulates our present role today and in the last few days. If I may quote from paragraph 64 of the Tadic judgement, "The two parties agree that a standard to be used when determining whether the Trial Chamber's factual finding should stand is that of unreasonableness, that is, a conclusion which no reasonable person could have reached. The task the hearing, assessing, and weighing the evidence presented at trial is left to the judges sitting in the Trial Chamber. Therefore, the Appeals Chamber must give a margin of deference to a finding of fact reached by a Trial Chamber. It is only where the evidence relied on by the Trial Chamber could not reasonably have been accepted by any reasonable person that the Appeals Chamber can substitute its own finding for that of the Trial Chamber. It is important to note that two judges both acting reasonably can come to different conclusions on the basis of the same evidence. In other words, to satisfy this burden, the appealing party would have to indicate clearly the nature of the error in the Trial Chamber's decision and to address fully the specific facts from the record of the trial that support its claim of error. A failure by the appealing party to discharge all or part of the relevant burden should result in the dismissal of the ground of appeal. In other words, the appellant who disputes the conclusion on appeal must persuade the Appeals Chamber that a conclusion is one which could not have reasonably been made by a reasonable tribunal of fact so that a miscarriage of justice has occurred." It is important, however, to put into the correct context the indictment of Vlatko Kupreskic. My learned colleague on the other side was correct when he said that a case involving Vlatko Kupreskic is different from the other appellants although, to my mind, in putting forward his position, he convoluted that ratio because to a large extent, the impression given in his submissions was that the evidence that is required to prove co-perpetration is of a similar ilk that is required to prove aiding and abetting. It is important at the onset to appreciate what is meant by aiding and abetting and what is meant by co-perpetration, because I think at the onset I should indicate that the defence case of Vlatko Kupreskic was to the effect that he was not present in the area when the persecutory incidents occurred; the specific acts alleged could not have possibly occurred; he did not consent to the use of his house by HVO soldiers; he didn't know about the persecutory campaign before it commenced; he could not have known of the preparations for such a campaign; he was not physically able to have committed the crimes alleged; and most of all, he was not the type of character that would have been involved in such a campaign. It is against this backdrop, but more emphatically against the ingredients of the offence on the indictment that we would look at what, in fact, the Prosecution had led in relation to Vlatko Kupreskic. Aiding and abetting is a residual form of participation that applies to all contributions of the criminal event that are not captured by planning, instigating, ordering, or committing as reflected by the language of Article 7(1). Although it is common to speak of aiding and abetting, the two concepts are distinct, and this was reflected in the Akayesu judgement at paragraph 484 to 485 -- my apology, paragraph 473, where they indicated that aiding means giving assistance to someone; abetting, on the other hand, would involve facilitating the commission of an act by being sympathetic thereto. Either aiding or abetting alone is sufficient to render the perpetrator criminally liable. So that as much as, in fact, there is the argument that mere presence cannot be an indicia or an indicator of complicity or cannot of itself per se be considered to be an aspect of aiding and abetting, it must be looked at in the context in which that evidence is led and all the other pertinent areas and pertinent facts that are supplied by the Prosecution in proof thereof. Thus, if mere presence at the scene of a crime is not per se sufficient to render an accused liable for aiding and abetting, presence during the commission of the crime can constitute abetting if it has an encouraging effect on the perpetrators or gives them moral support or psychological support, or a significant legitimising or encouraging effect on the principals. It is sufficient that the accused is aware of the substantial likelihood of the crime being committed by a member or members of a particular class of persons against a member or members of a particular class of potential victims. So that when one looks at this case from its factual matrix, it is important at the onset to indicate very categorically that a charge against Vlatko Kupreskic is aiding and abetting and not as a co-perpetrator. Granted, in fact, he was charged initially as being, in fact, part and parcel of the entire exercise, but those charges were dismissed. He was charged with aiding and abetting between the period of October 1992 and April 1993. So that it is important for the learned Tribunal to keep in focus the fact that the evidence that was led spread over a particular time period. As much as my friend has, in fact, indicated that this case is, in fact, based on circumstantial evidence, in respectful deference, it is the submission of the Prosecution that this case, apart from circumstantial evidence, is also based on direct evidence. And the state will go on to indicate why it is important to appreciate that it was, in fact, based on direct evidence. The indictment attributed three specific acts of persecution to the appellant in the context of aiding and abetting: deliberate and systematic killing of Bosnian Muslim civilians, the comprehensive destruction of Bosnian homes and property, the organised detention and expulsion from the Bosnian Muslim from Ahmici, Santici, and its environs. I don't think anyone can question that what happened in Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993 involved gross persecutory acts. What has to be established is the individual liability in the context of their role, and there are varying roles at that, because it is, in fact, the submission of the Prosecution, as found by the Trial Chamber, that the role of Vlatko Kupreskic was at a lower level, at an operative level, than what appeared in relation to the other appellants. It is important, however, to appreciate the difference between direct evidence and circumstantial evidence, because if, for example, the Tribunal is of the view that this case is based on circumstantial evidence, then it is circumscribed by the ratio to be found in Celebici with regard to how you interpret and to what extent you will give the required weight to circumstantial evidence. If I may refer the Court to page 5 -- to paragraph 986 to 987, where it is indicated in Celebici that a circumstantial case consists of evidence -- sorry, a circumstantial case consists of evidence of a number of different circumstances, when taken in combination, point to the guilt of the accused, because they would usually exist in combination only because the accused did what is alleged against him. Such a conclusion must be established beyond reasonable doubt. It is not sufficient that it is a reasonable conclusion available from that evidence. It must be the only reasonable conclusion available. If there is another conclusion which is also reasonably open from that evidence and which is consistent with the innocence of the accused, he must be acquitted. When one looks at the body of evidence that was adduced by the Prosecution, it is the submission of the Prosecution that it amounted to direct evidence. And that evidence consisted in the main of, 1, the unloading of weapons from a car in front of his home in October of 1992; 2, the fact that he was seen in front of the Hotel Vitez on the morning of the 15th of April, 1993 and in the early evening when a number of soldiers were seen in the vicinity of his house; 3, that there was troop activity in and around the appellant's home on the evening of the 15th of April, 1993, and this observation was confirmed by various witnesses; 4, the evidence of Witness H with regard to his role and in terms of his presence on the 16th of April, 1993 in the vicinity of the home of Suhret Ahmic; 5, that in fact he was involved in the preparations for the attack in his role as a police operations officer; and 6, that the Trial Chamber did in fact find that there was evidence that supported -- that he supported actions of others. It is important to note that all these contentious issues were, in fact, raised at trial, were seriously litigated at trial. And if one looks at the closing brief of Vlatko Kupreskic, one would appreciate that the very issues that have been raised here today in relation to whether the evidence is nebulous, is tenuous, was placed before the Trial Chamber and rejected. I'm not saying that the appellant cannot come now and not raise issues of fact in terms of the wrongful conclusions arrived at. The question that has to be asked: Has he in fact brought before this Chamber any additional evidence or any additional argument on the basis of the evidence that was before the Trial Chamber? And there is a resounding no. We're not dealing with the 115 evidence, we're dealing with the case as is, because this is why, in fact, I have decided not to approach it in this convoluted manner of chapters. I am dealing with the case in terms of sections, the case as is and the case now. This is why it is my intention to deal with the case now in open session and then possibly move into closed session when dealing with the additional evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I, in fact, at the break was about to indicate that in the closing brief, the appellant at paragraph 7, paragraph 26 to 31, 49 to 52, 60 to 64 in fact dealt with the whole issue with regard to his, the appellant's nationalist feelings and his role as a operations officer. The Trial Chamber considered it in paragraph 796. The Defence closing brief also dealt with evidence relating to the appellant's presents in Ahmici on the 15th of April, 1993. This was dealt with in the closing briefs, paragraph 14 to 19, 22 to 25, 53 to 55. Again, the Trial Chamber considered this in paragraph 797. The Defence closing brief dealt with the issue of the appellant's role in the preparations of the attack by allowing his house to be used a place for the troops in paragraphs 11 to 21, 56 to 62. Once more, the Trial Chamber dealt with those issues at paragraphs 798 to 799. In paragraph 802, the Trial Chamber concluded that the evidence of the accused as a witness as to his alleged lack of participation was not credible. In paragraph 803, the Trial Chamber summarises its consideration and concludes that the appellant assisted in the preparation and supported the attack carried out by the other accused, the HVO, and the military police. The Defence closing briefs dealt with this in paragraphs 35 to 46. So that the entire Defence case that we are hearing being put forward in the last two days with regard to evidence before the Trial Chamber, those matters are, in fact being relitigated and there is no additional argument in support of requesting the Court to decry the conclusions and determinations arrived at by the Trial Chamber. When one looks, for example, at Witness T, much as has been said about Witness T in regard to the unloading of arms into his house back in October of 1992. The fact of the matter is that the Appeals Chamber -- the Trial Chamber, my apology, did make findings that there were, indeed, skirmishes occurring between, in fact, the Muslim population and the Croats. And if one may consider, if I may extend it further, to the kind of fire power that came from Vlatko Kupreskic's house, from the warehouse, one may well see, for example, the relationship between that sighting and what occurred on the 16th of April, 1993. The fact of the matter is that this particular issue was heavily litigated. My learned friend has indicated that there was no explanation for with regard to what the weapons were, but on a studied look at the evidence given by T would reflect that the witness went on to indicate that the witness was referring to guns and, additionally, that it was just before dusk, it was some 50 metres away, and that, in fact, she saw the weapons, the guns, going into Vlatko Kupreskic's house. The fact that my learned friend has indicated and readily admitted that there was no cross-examination on that issue, and based his arguments on the premise that cross-examination ought to have taken place is, to my mind, revisiting an issue that has already been litigated in the 115 motion that dealt with the issue of adversarial incompetence because my friend cannot afford to fall prey to a 115 motion deja vu in returning to issues that have been, in fact, adjudicated upon. Because he says, for example, startlingly there was no cross-examination of Witness T on the point to test the reliability of the observation. What is he getting that when he said there was no CXC? What, in fact, is quite obvious that the attorney then realised that to further clarify the issue with regard to the weapons that was taking place would have been quite damaging to the appellant and as a result, rightfully or justifiably so, given the unity of identity between counsel and client which the Tribunal invokes upon on all occasions, they decided not to further cross-examination. Because, let us be blunt here, the issue of flagrant adversarial incompetence does not arise in these proceedings. With regard to the issue of identification, reference has been made to the sighting of Vlatko Kupreskic outside the Vitez police station, the Vitez Hotel on the 15th between 2.00 and 3.00 in the afternoon. I do agree with my friend that the Court, in its assessing of the evidence, simply states what the evidence is in a very matter of fact way. Yes, he was seen in the company of two or three soldiers outside Vitez. But, again, I do besiege the learned Tribunal to have a read of these individuals witnesses, I am talking about T, B, L, O. When one reads these I transcripts, you recognise that what, in fact, the learned Trial Chamber was doing was encapsulating the evidence on the particular umbrella head. When, for example, you read about a particular witness who said that, in fact, she saw soldiers going into the basement, a very significant piece of evidence that is not mentioned on the record but is part of the evidence was to the effect that they were dressed in military gear. "I saw them come out into the basement and they disappeared." "Where did they go?" "There was a warehouse right next door." And when one looks at the treatise of facts that were led by the Prosecution, one would recognise that the greatest fire power came from those two particular areas. My friend made mention of, in fact, the use of experts, Professor Wagenaar in terms of the need to appreciate what, in fact, he was saying, but the Trial Chamber did appreciate what he was saying. I bring to your attention the fact that they did not believe Q who had said, for example, that Vlatko was firing at some hapless victim because they appreciated what Professor Wagenaar said with regard to distance and there was no corroboration. In the same vein they are expected to have appreciated what he was saying in the evaluation of all the identification evidence so that the fact that it is not mentioned per se does not necessarily mean that it wasn't considered in the same way that one heavy weather is made of my friend in relation to the fact that no mention is made of Mirko Vidovic, but you would remember that the Trial Chamber had to deal with the similar issue in relation to EE that, in fact, it dealt with the question of inconsistent identification in relation to other individuals. So the fact that it was not mentioned, however, the fact that it was raised in very significant terms in the closing brief by the appellant, and the fact that the Trial Chamber had to deal with the similar issue in relation to the other appellant is an indication that they were quite privy to the dilemma to that, in fact, whole question with relation to identification and that they resolve it taking into consideration the principles, the very principles invoked by my learned friend. In any event, the very principle of Turnbull is subject to limitations because I have, in fact, lodged two other cases that illustrate quite succinctly that it is only to be dealt with cases of fleeting glances and it is not to be considered as a type of catechism, a type of mantra that the courts must follow at all times. Your Honour, you would appreciate that given the constraints of time I will have to indicate to the Court that I will be adopting my arguments in its entirety in terms of issues in relation to what transpired. Now, it is important to note that my friend, my learned colleague cannot, in fact, lead evidence from the bar table. When the witness says that, "I saw the individual outside the Vitez police station," it cannot be suggested that because he has a supermarket down there, he may have been there. Because that is not the evidence. The evidence of the appellant is that "I was not there." And in that regard, my learned friend cannot approbate and reprobate. You cannot, for example, say, "Listen, if I was there is because I was going to my supermarket. But if you believe, in fact, I was there, at the same point in time, I was not there." The same thing occurs in relation to the sighting of H -- by H of Vlatko Kupreskic at 5.30 in the morning. My friend makes the suggestion from the bar table that: Well, it may be that he was coming from the Verbeck shelter at around that time. He was coming, and maybe that is why he was identified as being there at that particular time but there is an error of fact on that proposition because the witness is saying that I saw him at about 5.30 to 5.45 when Vlatko Kupreskic was coming from the shelter. It was at 10.00 a.m. in the morning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: And the reason why my friend, in fact, is probably putting forward that position, it may well be because of his belief that the evidence against him is circumstantial. So there must be inferences. There must be reasonable inferences. And based on that, definitely in those circumstances, the inference most favourable to the accused you would adopt, to the appellant. But when one looks at the entire case in the context of the preparations on that particular day, you would appreciate, Your Honour, that as I said before, Witnesses T, B, L, M shows individuals arriving there dressed as soldiers going into the house, being seen on the balcony and all those other places. I may say in passing that the only presence, the only presence that has been advocated by AT has no real relevance to this particular issue because AT was not there. And the only witness, in fact, who can probably seriously confront that particular issue is ADA. And it is a submission of the Prosecution that the very evidence of ADA fails on its own admission. His was, in fact, an exercise in shifts. I have, in fact, already mapped out in very incisive terms, my friend refers to as, in fact, in the context of heat, but I do agree with him it is a lot of heat and at the end of the day you would appreciate, Your Honours, that that particular witness was one that in fact could not be believed in the circumstances in terms of the kind of evidence that he had. It is not my intention to go in en masse in terms of the type of facts that he spoke about because I am pressed for time, but in my brief, I have outlined some of those areas of concern. In passing, I should indicate that the Defence of the appellant was indeed an alibi, and the Prosecution led evidence to rebut that alibi. One would appreciate, for example, that the evidence in relation to ADA, if I may start to impinge on that aspect of the case is -- has a very selective process in that it is what is often referred to as negative evidence. Because one would appreciate, and I have, in fact, left with the learned tribunal a particular case on alibi that indicates what is considered to be evidence in support of alibi. That is -- that has to be something of an affirmative nature. What is the position of the Prosecution is to the effect that the evidence of ADA who says basically, listen, I did not see him. To all intents and purposes, it is negative evidence. It is not as strong as the affirmative evidence that was led by the Defence which was rejected by the Trial Chamber by Ljubica Kupreskic, by Ivica Kupreskic, and by various other witnesses. And the case I refer to is R. And Johnson. It is part of my brief. Your Honours, if I may in fact at this time request closed session I am about to deal ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: I'm much obliged. You're dealing with juridical minds, minds that, in fact, encompass a level of analysis that one would not find among laypeople. So that when, for example, the Trial Chamber, for example, puts in very bullet form what the facts were, it is a far cry from saying that is the evidence. We need to go further and look and see what -- how that evidence came out and in what context. I'm not saying, by any stretch of the imagination, that you ought to believe everything that a particular witness says based on that approach; but certainly in looking at the context in which it was said, one would, in fact, juridically determine that when the Court said, "I saw him in front of Vitez," they were in fact referring to that particular instant where the officer made rounds with his car. He said, in fact, he was driving very slowly. Everyone looks at the type of evidence led in relation to the preparation. When you look at all these witnesses, you will appreciate that half of the evidence that relates to the conflagration is not mentioned because it is all done under this bullet form. Obviously, the Trial Chamber was in a position to look at the demeanor of witnesses as you have been in a position to look at the demeanor of all the additional evidence, and you can make a finding in terms of credibility. It is the position of the appellant -- of the Prosecution that the evidence that has been led so far in relation to the 115 is not of that ilk, to disturb the determinative findings of the Trial Chamber. Because when you bring evidence before an Appeal Chamber, it must be evidence that has a particular bona fides. You cannot come and rationalise and say all the witnesses are exaggerating, that that witness, in fact, was eccentric. When, for example, you cannot tell the Trial Chamber that this witness is to be believed, it is an indication that you appreciate the exceptional standards that are required before an Appeal Chamber can reverse the findings of a Trial Chamber. In those circumstances, it is the submission of the Prosecution that -- as I said, I adopt en masse my submissions in the brief that the Prosecution has filed, and it is the position that there is no merit in the submissions by my learned friend that the particular evidence would have vitiated or mitigated the evidence that the Trial Chamber would have heard. In any event, the bottom line, as I have said initially, the test is reasonableness, the reasonableness in the evaluation process of a Trial Chamber. Can we -- could we or can we fault them if, in fact, they have heard that evidence? Because I can assure you it is the submission that had they heard the evidence of ADA, they would have, in fact, rejected it; had they heard the evidence of AT, they would have, in fact, appreciated that his knowledge would have, in fact, suffered from certain delimitations. Your Honours, this is essentially the arguments of the Prosecution on this core.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Carmona.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Any questions? I think not. So the Prosecution can proceed on to the next stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: I'm much obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
